tagline.text: A Bohol resort island where dawn dolphins and white sand await

items.credit: A.C.T. Alejandre / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: An island connected by bridge to the southwest of mainland Bohol, and Bohol's travel hub — resorts, dive shops, and restaurants cluster around Alona Beach. Dawn dolphin hopping, snorkeling at Balicasag Island, and cave-pool swimming are all within a day's reach.

Panglao Island is about 90 km² and sits right off Tagbilaran, the capital of mainland Bohol, connected to it by two bridges. The island is divided into Dauis to the east and Panglao to the west; most travelers stay around Alona Beach on the island's southwest side. When Bohol–Panglao International Airport opened on the island in
, direct flights from Manila and Korea became possible, and resort development has expanded quickly since then.
Alona Beach is a white sand beach about
1.5km

long, densely lined with resorts, dive shops, restaurants, and bars. It isn't as large as Boracay, but its big advantage is a coral wall just offshore, meaning good dive sites are only a few minutes away by boat. Doljo Beach on the island's northwest side and the beaches around Doljo/Dauis to the southeast are quieter than Alona and popular with those wanting a peaceful holiday.

The highlight of a Panglao trip is the dawn hopping tour. The classic route is to head out by bangka before sunrise near Pamilacan Island to look for spinner dolphins, then snorkel at Balicasag Island, where sea turtles are common, and finish with photos on the Virgin Island sandbar that emerges at low tide. The island also has limestone cave pools such as Hinagdanan Cave and a Spanish-era church, so there's plenty to enjoy beyond the beach.

A resort destination quieter than Cebu and closer than Boracay, it has steadily won over Korean families, honeymooners, and divers. Inland Bohol attractions such as the Chocolate Hills and the Loboc River are only
1–2 hours
away by car, making it a great base for combining relaxation with sightseeing.
Boats leave Alona Beach around
to look for spinner dolphins in the waters around Pamilacan Island. Dolphins are wild, so sightings aren't guaranteed every time, but the odds are good on dry-season mornings.
A marine protected area about
30–40 minutes
from Alona by boat, where you can see sea turtles, schools of jackfish, and a colorful coral wall. A guide is mandatory.

A sandbar that emerges long and narrow in the middle of the sea at low tide, where you can see sea urchins and starfish and take great photos. It's mostly submerged at high tide, so visits are timed to the tide.
The coral wall just off Alona Beach is a popular spot for beginner trial dives and certification courses. Several dive shops here have Korean-speaking instructors.
Descending along the sea cliffs at Napaling on the island's northwest coast, you can snorkel over a swirling school of millions of sardines.
Hinagdanan Cave in Dauis is a limestone cave lit by sunlight through an opening in the ceiling, with a clear underground pool for swimming.

The Church of Our Lady of the Assumption on the Dauis coast is an elegant church built of coral stone, known for a story that its well beneath the altar stays fresh, not salty, despite being right by the sea.

The area around Alona Beach is walkable, and getting around the island otherwise means tricycles (about
for a short ride), Grab, or motorbike rental (about
a day). Book hopping-tour boats through a beach tour booth or your accommodation.
The dry season,
December–May
, is best, and especially
March–May
is ideal for hopping and diving thanks to calm seas and good visibility.
December–February
can bring afternoon wind from the northeast monsoon, but the cooler temperatures are pleasant.
June–November

is the rainy season with frequent showers, though it doesn't usually rain all day. Bohol is a bit off the main typhoon path compared with Luzon, but when a typhoon or tropical depression passes through between
October and December
, hopping tours and fast craft can be cancelled.

During peak Korean travel periods — Lunar New Year, summer vacation, Chuseok — as well as Philippine Holy Week and the Christmas holidays, resort rates rise and hopping boats get crowded. If you want to see dolphins quietly, choose a boat that departs as early as possible.

The most convenient area to stay is Alona Beach. Beachfront resorts run about
or more a night, while hotels and guesthouses in the lanes
5–10 minutes
inland from the beach run about

. For a quiet retreat, the large resorts on Doljo Beach to the north or in Dauis/Dumaluan to the east are good, though these areas are structured around dining within the resort, so restaurant choices are limited.

Alona Beach has a wide range of restaurants beyond Filipino food, including Korean, Italian, and Spanish. Every evening, beach restaurants lay out fish, shrimp, and squid on ice for a seafood barbecue priced by weight — a local specialty. The long-running Bohol Bee Farm is famous for organic salads, flower-topped dishes, and homemade ice cream, and is worth a stop for a meal or souvenir shopping. Among local dishes, be sure to try kinilaw, calamay, and mango desserts.
There are several ATMs around Alona Beach, but cash can still run out on busy weekends during peak season. Hopping tours and environmental fees are often cash-only.

Chartering your own boat for a hopping tour gives you more control over the schedule than joining a shared tour with other travelers. For a family of 4–6, chartering can cost about the same per person as joining a group tour.
Balicasag snorkeling is only available on small guided boats, and due to capacity limits, going early in the morning means a shorter wait.
At low tide, the water at Alona Beach recedes and seaweed can be exposed. Swimming is best around high tide.
Tour prices offered by beach touts are negotiable. Be sure to confirm what's included — environmental fee, snorkel gear, lunch.
Good photo spots are the Virgin Island sandbar, the sunset at the cliffs on the west end of Alona Beach, and the light beams in Hinagdanan Cave.
Smart and Globe signal is good island-wide, and you can buy a SIM card at the airport.
Multiple boats crowding around dolphins to chase them causes the animals great stress. Don't approach closely or feed them — keep your distance and observe.
Touching or stepping on sea turtles and coral is prohibited and can result in a fine if caught.
There are sea urchins and cone snails in the beach and sea, so don't walk barefoot over coral areas.
Local ordinances govern beach smoking, drinking, and noise. Smoke only in designated areas.
Wearing a helmet and carrying an international driving permit are required when renting a motorbike. Roads are dark at night and dogs often dart out.
Midday UV is very strong. Bring reef-safe sunscreen and a rash guard.
